how-much-does-a-land-survey-cost.html.text:
← Land Survey Bid Calculator

How much does a land survey cost?

Far less than acreage decides, and far more than corner count decides. A 5-acre parcel with lost corners in heavy woods can price higher than a 40-acre parcel with easy corners and a clean title — the opposite of what a per-acre rate assumes.

The same 5 acres, three different corner stories

Using this calculator's own verified defaults for everything except corner count, condition, and terrain:

ParcelField hoursPriceFlat $120/acre quote
5 ac, 4 easy corners to locate, open terrain1.67$1,084.82$600.00
5 ac, 3 locate + 1 set, moderate terrain (defaults)3.03$1,274.05$600.00
5 ac, 4 corners to set, heavy terrain8.07$1,970.97$600.00

Every row is the same 5 acres. A flat per-acre rate quotes all three at $600.00; the actual price ranges from $1,084.82 to $1,970.97 — corner count and terrain, not acreage, decide where in that range a job falls.

A small, hard parcel can cost more than a large, easy one

A 40-acre parcel with 4 easy corners, open terrain, and only 1 hour of title research prices at this calculator's $850.00 minimum job fee — about 82% less than the $4,800.00 a flat $120/acre rate would quote for 40 acres. The 5-acre parcel with 4 corners to set in heavy terrain above prices at $1,970.97, more than double the large parcel's price, on an eighth of the acreage. Acreage alone predicts neither number.

What this is not

This is arithmetic on the rates and corner counts you type. It does not perform a legal boundary determination, check any state's minimum technical standards, or replace a licensed surveyor's own professional judgment about scope, liability, or errors and omissions coverage. Replace every rate with your own invoices before relying on either number.

No warranty. This free page is not surveying, engineering, or legal advice. You are responsible for reviewing and verifying its output before relying on it. It is hosted best-effort with no SLA: it may be slow, broken, moved, or taken offline without notice. Open the bid calculator to price a specific parcel.

Common questions

How much does a land survey cost?

It depends far more on corner count and condition than on acreage. On this calculator's own verified defaults (5 acres, 3 corners to locate, 1 to set, moderate terrain), a survey prices around $1,274.05 — more than double a flat $120/acre quote for the same parcel ($600.00). A small, difficult parcel can price higher still than a large, easy one.

Why can a small parcel cost more than a large one?

Because field time is driven by corners, not acres. A 5-acre parcel with all 4 corners needing to be set from scratch in heavy terrain prices around $1,970.97 on this calculator's defaults — more than double a 40-acre parcel with 4 easy-to-locate corners in open terrain and a light research load, which prices at the $850.00 minimum job fee.

How much more does setting a corner cost versus locating one?

On the same 5-acre parcel, switching all corners from “to locate” in open terrain to “to set” in heavy terrain raises the field-hours figure from 1.67 to 8.07 — nearly 5x — because setting a corner with no recoverable monument means resolving its position from the deed and running a traverse to it, field time a flat per-acre rate has no line for.

Does a bigger parcel always cost more to survey?

No. On this calculator's defaults, a 40-acre parcel with 4 easy corners, open terrain, and 1 hour of research prices at the $850.00 minimum job fee — about 82% less than the $4,800.00 a flat $120/acre rate would have quoted for that acreage, because the corners and research drove almost no field or office time regardless of how many acres they sit on.

Hand the customer a proposal

The price above is for you. This is the page you print or save as a PDF and give to the customer — your details, their details, the scope, the deposit split, and a line for them to sign. Private by default

Everything on this page runs in your browser and nothing is ever uploaded. There is no account and no server-side storage of any kind — your parcel details, corner counts, rates, and price are never saved or sent anywhere, and refreshing the page clears them by design. We count only anonymous local feature events (quote_calculated, reset, sponsor_link_clicked) so we can tell whether the calculator gets used — no parcel, price, or client figures are recorded, and Do Not Track / Global Privacy Control turn it off automatically.

Common questions

Is this a legal boundary determination or a substitute for my professional judgment?

No. This is a pricing worksheet only. It does not perform a legal boundary determination, does not check any state's minimum technical standards, and does not replace your own professional judgment about scope, liability, or errors-and-omissions coverage on a given job.

Why does the calculator separate corners to locate from corners to set?

Locating an existing, recoverable monument is a confirmation against a physical marker. Setting a corner with no recoverable monument means resolving the position from the deed and record research and then running and holding a traverse to it with nothing to check it against on the ground — field time this calculator prices noticeably higher per corner, because it usually is.

Why not just quote per acre like most of the trade does?

Acreage does not see corner count, whether corners must be set or just located, or how tangled the title chain is. A small parcel with several lost corners and a messy deed history can cost more to survey than a large, clean, open one — so a flat per-acre number gets one of them wrong. The comparison panel below shows the gap on the job you just priced.

Does anything about my job or client get uploaded?

No. Every number on this page runs in your browser only. Nothing is sent to a server, there is no account, and no parcel address, client name, or price is ever saved or transmitted. Usage counting only tallies anonymous feature events, and you can turn it off below.

What if I don't know the exact corner count or research hours before I bid?

Use your best estimate from the plat, prior surveys of adjoining parcels, or a quick record-search pass before quoting — the same way you would size up any job. This tool prices the numbers you enter; it does not verify them against the deed itself.

vs-a-flat-per-acre-quote.html.text:
← Land Survey Bid Calculator

This calculator vs. a flat per-acre quote

"$120 an acre" is not a price for a survey — it is a price for one specific corner count, corner condition, and research load, quietly applied to every parcel that calls in.

What a flat per-acre rate is

A flat per-acre rate is the fastest way to quote: multiply the parcel's acreage by a number and read off a price. Clients shop it because it is easy to compare between bids, and it is the number a client holding a neighbor's old survey or a competitor's quote will ask you to match.

The number behind it was set for one job — one corner count, one corner condition (all recoverable, none set from scratch), one research load, no unusual terrain — and then reused for every parcel afterward, whether or not the next parcel looks anything like the one the rate was built on.

What this calculator is

This page keeps no account and sends nothing to a server. You enter how many corners have to be located versus set from scratch, the terrain, how many hours of deed/plat/easement research the title chain needs, your crew's loaded rate, and drafting and travel costs. It converts corner count and condition into field hours, adds research and drafting separately, and returns a walk-away price below which the job loses money — for this parcel, not a generic one.

What a flat per-acre rate doesWhat this calculator does instead
Charges the same $/acre whether every corner is an easy, recoverable monument or several have to be set from scratch — two to three times the field time per corner. Prices corners to locate and corners to set separately, at their own base field minutes, before the terrain multiplier is applied.
Prices "the parcel" as one number, with no separate line for how much deed, plat, or easement research the title chain actually needs. Times record research at an hourly rate the surveyor enters, so a tangled 1950s deed chain costs more than a clean, recent one.
Applies one multiplier (or none at all) regardless of whether access is open and cleared or heavy woods and wetland. Applies a terrain multiplier to field time directly, so a heavy-access job prices differently from an open, easy one.
A ten-acre parcel with six easy corners and a clean title chain and a two-acre infill lot with three lost corners and a tangled deed price the same. The ten-acre parcel and the two-acre lot price on their own corners, terrain, and research — not on acreage, so the two jobs come out differently priced.
Gives the surveyor a number to quote, not a number to check a quote against. Reports the walk-away price and the dollar/percent gap against what a flat per-acre rate would have quoted the same job, so a shopped price can be scored against real cost before the surveyor commits to it.

Two parcels, the same acreage-blind rate

Using this calculator's own defaults and a $120/acre naive rate:

ParcelFlat per-acre quoteCorner-and-research-driven priceGap
40 acres, 2 easy corners to locate, open terrain, 1 hour of research$4,800$850 (the calculator's minimum job fee)The flat rate overcharges by about $3,950 — 82% too high.
2 acres, 1 corner to locate and 3 to set, heavy terrain, 8 hours of research$240$2,473The flat rate undercharges by about $2,233 — the job needs more than nine times that quote.

Both parcels use the same $120/acre naive rate. The gap runs in either direction because acreage is not the driver — corner count, corner condition, terrain, and research are. Run your own parcel's numbers in the calculator to see which side of the gap it falls on.

A flat rate is not wrong because it is simple — it is wrong when it is applied outside the one job it was built for, and nothing about a per-acre number tells you when that has happened. This calculator does not replace judgment about your market; it replaces the arithmetic a flat rate skips.

Common questions

Why does a flat per-acre rate get a survey quote wrong?

Because field time comes from corner count and condition, not from acreage. A large, open parcel with a few easy-to-locate corners can take far less field time than a small, brushy parcel with several corners that have to be set from scratch, but a per-acre rate charges the large parcel more every time.

What does a per-acre rate usually leave out entirely?

Record research. A clean title chain with recent, consistent deeds is a fast research pass; a tangled chain going back decades, or one with unresolved easements, can add hours before anyone drives to the site. Acreage says nothing about which one a given parcel is.

What happens when a corner has no recoverable monument?

Setting a corner with nothing to check it against on the ground means resolving its position from the deed and record research, then running and holding a traverse to it — field time that can run two to three times what confirming an existing, recoverable monument takes. A flat per-acre rate cannot tell how many of a parcel's corners fall into which category.

Is a flat per-acre rate ever the right way to quote?

For a narrow band of near-identical jobs — similar corner count and condition, similar terrain, similar research load — a per-acre rate can land close. The risk is applying it outside that band without noticing, because the rate does not know which band a given parcel is in and neither does the surveyor until the corners and the title chain are actually reviewed.

Does this calculator know what to charge in my market?

No. It has no data on local rates or what competitors charge. It takes the crew rate, office rate, and travel costs you enter and turns them into a walk-away price for the corners, terrain, and research you describe — the arithmetic a flat per-acre rate skips, not a market survey.

Nothing here says or implies that quoting a flat rate per acre is a bad-faith practice — it is a common, honest shortcut that works until the job stops matching the one the rate was set on. This page describes where that shortcut breaks down, not a fault in anyone who uses it.
